<p class="interior-lede">I’m a computational scientist interested in the places where chemistry becomes collective: at interfaces, in solution, and across the noisy trajectories produced by molecular simulation.</p>

::: {.content-section}
## What I do

My research combines statistical physics, high-performance molecular simulation, and modern machine learning. I build models that connect microscopic motion to experimentally meaningful observables—especially electric fields, solvent organization, and electrochemical response at solid–liquid interfaces.

I’m most at home when a problem demands several kinds of thinking at once: physical theory to frame the question, computation to test it, and careful inference to separate signal from noise.
:::

::: {.content-section}
## How I work

::: {.principle-grid}
::: {.principle-card}
### Physics first

Start from the symmetries, limits, and mechanisms that make a model interpretable.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
### Computation with purpose

Use simulation and machine learning as instruments for answering a precise scientific question.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
### Reproducible by design

Build transparent workflows that make results easier to test, extend, and reuse.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
### Across disciplines

Translate ideas between chemistry, physics, biology, and data science without losing the details that matter.
:::
:::
:::

## Background

### Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Postdoctoral associate, 2020–2025. Research spanning interfacial electric fields, Bayesian inference, molecular simulation, and scientific computing.

::: {.fact-card}
### University of Maine

PhD in physical chemistry (2020), following a BS in chemistry. Doctoral work explored molecular behavior in confined systems and ligand-mediated nanomaterials.
